slides.action_title: A world-class compiler has been dying in silence for five years.
key_points: Toyama Prefecture: One engineer, alone
High-performance EVM compiler in Haskell
Advanced formal verification and optimization
Five years. Zero collaborators.
slides.speaker_notes: Let me tell you about someone you've never heard of. In Toyama Prefecture, there is an engineer who has been building a world-class EVM compiler for five years. It's written in Haskell. It features advanced formal verification capabilities and sophisticated optimization techniques. This is exactly the kind of work that would attract attention at any top research institution in the world. But here's the thing: he's been doing it completely alone. No collaborators. No community. No one to discuss ideas with. For five years. This isn't a story about one person's failure. This is a story about a system that fails its best people. And I suspect some of you in this room know exactly what that isolation feels like.
slides.anecdote_used: Used the Toyama Haskell engineer story from CONTEXT_BRIEF to personalize the opening and create emotional resonance.

slides.action_title: This is not one engineer's failure—it is a symptom of a system.
key_points: University operating grants: -140 billion yen since 2004
1% annual efficiency coefficient compounding for 20 years
Research collaboration opportunities shrinking
Academia and industry operating in silos
slides.speaker_notes: That engineer in Toyama is not an outlier. He is a symptom. Since 2004, national university operating grants have been cut by approximately 140 billion yen—that's not a one-time cut, that's a 1% annual efficiency coefficient compounding year after year for two decades. What does that mean in practice? It means fewer opportunities to attend conferences. Fewer chances for cross-institutional collaboration. It means academia and industry operating in separate silos, rarely talking to each other. And it means talented people like that Toyama engineer working in isolation, their potential slowly evaporating. This is not a personal problem. This is a structural problem. And I believe many of you have felt it.
slides.anecdote_used: Extended the Toyama engineer story to connect individual experience to systemic issues.

slides.action_title: Japan has fallen from 4th to 10th in global research impact—and the decline continues.
key_points: Top 10% highly-cited papers: 4th → 10th place
Total papers ranking: 2nd → 4th place
NIRA warning: 'Japanese science itself will decline'
The trajectory is not stabilizing
slides.speaker_notes: Let me give you the numbers, because the numbers are alarming. Twenty years ago, Japan ranked 4th in the world for Top 10% highly-cited papers. Today, we rank 10th. In total research papers, we've dropped from 2nd to 4th. And the NIRA research institute has issued a stark warning: if this isolation continues, and I quote, 'Japanese science itself will decline.' These are not abstract statistics. This is our trajectory. And the trajectory is not flattening—it's still pointing down. We are watching Japanese research excellence erode in real time. The question is: what do we do about it?

slides.action_title: We call it the Isolation Tax—and every researcher in this room is paying it.
key_points: The Isolation Tax: the invisible cost of working alone
No cross-institutional networks
No global research community connections
Brilliant work that never finds its audience
slides.speaker_notes: I want to give this problem a name. We call it the Isolation Tax. It's the invisible cost that every researcher in Japan pays when they work in isolation. It's the paper that could have been a breakthrough if you'd had someone to discuss it with. It's the collaboration that never happened because you never met the right person. It's the funding opportunity you never heard about because you weren't connected to the right network. When I was doing my master's, I had almost no opportunity to interact with students from other universities in the same field. I thought that was normal. I thought that was just how research worked. It took me years to realize: that's not normal. That's the Isolation Tax. And every person in this room has paid it, whether you realize it or not.
slides.anecdote_used: Used the founder's personal experience of having no opportunity to interact with students from other universities during their master's program.

slides.action_title: Meanwhile, Ethereum's research frontier is rich with unsolved problems—and funding.
key_points: Ethereum: a trillion-yen-scale global system
Ethereum Foundation PSE RFP list: open research grants
Abundant funding for serious cryptography research
Problems that matter to millions of users
slides.speaker_notes: Now let me show you something completely different. While Japanese researchers struggle with shrinking budgets and isolation, there is a global research ecosystem that most of you have never encountered. Ethereum is a trillion-yen-scale system with real users, real stakes, and real problems that need solving. The Ethereum Foundation's PSE team has published an RFP list—that's a Request for Proposals list—with research grant opportunities specifically for cryptography and formal verification work. This is not a closed club. This is an open invitation. And here's what surprised me when I first discovered it: almost no one at SCIS knows about this. The funding is there. The problems are there. The connection is missing.

slides.action_title: These are not toy problems—they are publication-worthy challenges in cryptography and formal verification.
key_points: Zero-knowledge proof systems optimization
Formal verification of smart contracts
Cryptographic protocol security analysis
Problems that advance the field, not just the product
slides.speaker_notes: I know what some of you might be thinking. Blockchain research? Is this serious cryptography, or is it industry hype? Let me be clear: these are not toy problems. The challenges in the Ethereum ecosystem are exactly the kind of problems that get published in top venues. Zero-knowledge proof systems that need optimization. Formal verification techniques for smart contract security. Cryptographic protocol analysis with real adversarial conditions. This is work that advances the field of cryptography itself, not just a commercial product. I say this because I respect your standards. You didn't become cryptography researchers to do superficial work. Neither did we. The problems are worthy of your expertise.

slides.action_title: Our team has already found 20+ vulnerabilities in Ethereum clients—rigorous work gets recognized here.
key_points: Nyx Foundation: 20+ vulnerabilities discovered in Ethereum clients
Invited lectures at EF formal verification camp
Joint research with Ethereum Foundation
Rigorous work gets recognized and funded
slides.speaker_notes: This is not theoretical. Let me tell you what our team has already done. Nyx Foundation has reported over 20 vulnerabilities in Ethereum client implementations. This is rigorous security research that has had real impact on a system used by millions of people. Our founder has delivered invited lectures at the Ethereum Foundation's formal verification camp. We've conducted joint research with the EF. The point I want you to understand is this: when you do rigorous work in this ecosystem, it gets recognized. It gets funded. It gets amplified to a global audience. The bridge from Japanese academia to this world is not a fantasy. We've already crossed it. And we're here to help you cross it too.
slides.anecdote_used: Referenced founder's journey including ZK Tokyo, EF collaboration, and invited lectures to demonstrate proof of concept.

slides.action_title: The Nyx Foundation community exists to connect you to these problems—starting today.
key_points: Nyx Foundation: a bridge, not a gatekeeper
Deep Ethereum expertise and global network
Support for navigating research grants and RFPs
The connection starts with a conversation
slides.speaker_notes: So what is Nyx Foundation, and why are we here? We are not a company trying to sell you something. We are a community that exists to be a bridge. Our founder broke away from the traditional path specifically to dismantle the walls isolating Japanese researchers. We founded the ZK Tokyo community. We built deep expertise and a global network within Ethereum. And now we're extending that bridge to you. If you're interested in exploring the PSE RFP list, we can help you navigate it. If you have research ideas that might fit the Ethereum ecosystem, we can help you connect with the right people. The bridge exists. It's real. And crossing it can start with a single conversation.
slides.anecdote_used: Referenced founder's explicit mission statement: 'I myself leaped into the outside world to break down these walls.'

slides.action_title: At DEPCON Hakodate, professors, students, and EF researchers are already collaborating across borders.
key_points: DEPCON Hakodate: a model of what's possible
University professors, graduate students, corporate researchers
Ethereum Foundation researchers, Taiwan community members
Cross-institutional, cross-national collaboration happening now
slides.speaker_notes: Let me give you a concrete example of what this collaboration looks like in practice. DEPCON Hakodate brings together university professors, graduate students, corporate researchers, Ethereum Foundation researchers, and members of the Taiwan Ethereum community. All in one room. Discussing problems together. This is not a vision for the future—this is already happening. The walls that separate institutions, that separate countries, that separate academia from industry—at DEPCON, those walls come down. And the research that emerges from these collaborations is stronger because of it. The founder's conviction is that 'the era of researching alone or with just a few people is coming to an end.' DEPCON is proof that the new era is already beginning.
slides.anecdote_used: Referenced founder's vision that 'the era of researching alone or with just a few people is coming to an end.'

slides.action_title: End the isolation. Start the collaboration.
key_points: The Isolation Tax is not inevitable
The bridge to global research exists
Winning together through cooperation
Your next step: reach out to Nyx Foundation
slides.speaker_notes: The Isolation Tax is not a law of nature. It's a consequence of broken systems and missing connections. And connections can be built. Today, I've shown you that there is a global research ecosystem with funding, with compelling problems, and with people who want to collaborate with Japanese researchers. I've shown you that Nyx Foundation has already built the bridge. All that remains is for you to decide whether to cross it. We're not asking you to abandon your current work or your current institution. We're inviting you to expand your horizons. To find collaborators you've never met. To tackle problems that matter on a global scale. The founder's phrase captures it perfectly: 'winning together through cooperation.' That's the future we're building. And we would be honored to build it with you. Find us after this talk, or reach out to Nyx Foundation. End the isolation. Start the collaboration.
slides.anecdote_used: Used founder's phrase 'winning together through cooperation' to close with the core vision.

speaker_notes_are_complete_paragraphs.justification: All speaker notes are written as complete, flowing paragraphs that provide context, narrative, and transitions. They are not bullet points read aloud but rather a guide for what the presenter should actually say, including emotional cues, rhetorical questions, and personal touches.

anecdotes_incorporated.justification: Both key anecdotes from the CONTEXT_BRIEF have been incorporated: (1) The Toyama Haskell engineer story is used prominently in slides 1-2 as the emotional opening hook, (2) The founder's personal experience of isolation during their master's program is used in slide 4 to name the Isolation Tax. Additionally, the founder's journey and vision are woven throughout slides 7-10.

collaborative_framing_used.justification: Throughout the presentation, partnerships are framed collaboratively rather than prescriptively. Examples: 'The community collaborates on research priorities' (not 'PSE sets the agenda'), 'we can help you navigate' (not 'we will direct you'), 'we're inviting you to expand your horizons' (not 'you should join us'), and 'we would be honored to build it with you' (not 'you need to participate'). The call to action respects autonomy: 'decide whether to cross it.'
